target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
proof:
This is a reduction of the configured exercise, including its disclosed support interpretation. Its hypotheses are exactly the original ones: integers n,m≥1; a jointly C∞ map on ℝⁿ×(0,∞); a fixed Euclidean unit vector q; unit length of u; pointwise normality of u_tt−Δu with a merely existential real scalar at each point; and for every 0<s<t a compact spatial C_[s,t] outside which u=q throughout [s,t]. No regularity of that scalar, initial data, common compact set for all positive times, or support assumption on u itself is added. The required conclusion includes integrability and differentiability of the finite integral as well as its zero derivative.

1. Coordinate representation (part of B010).
Identify ℝⁿ and ℝᵐ with functions on Fin n and Fin m in their fixed standard coordinates. Use canonical Lebesgue volume on Fin n→ℝ, which is the product of the usual one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. This is the given dx, with no Jacobian, normalization factor or change of basis. On the finite coordinate spaces the product norm topology agrees with the Euclidean topology; differentiability and C∞ regularity are therefore the original ones. Define dot(v,w)=∑_k v_k w_k and normSq(v)=dot(v,v). In particular normSq is the Euclidean norm squared, regardless of the norm used for the ambient Lean function type. Thus normSq q=1 and UnitValued express exactly the original unit constraints, not a supremum norm constraint. Extend u arbitrarily to t≤0, for example by q there, solely to give total Lean functions. The open set U={(x,t):0<t} contains all points where any assertion is made. Smooth means ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ on U, not analyticity, and imposes no regularity on this extension at zero. Restriction of a total representative and arbitrary extension give both directions of the representation of the original half-space map. Derivatives at positive times are local and hence independent of the extension.

The header defines V=u_t, A=u_tt, P_j=∂_j u, S_j=∂_jj u, L=∑_j S_j, e=dot(V,V)+∑_j dot(P_j,P_j), E(t)=∫ e(x,t) dx. All component derivatives use ordinary real deriv or fderiv evaluated at the standard vector e_j=Pi.single j 1. In particular L is exactly the componentwise Laplacian, and e uses the Frobenius square with coefficient 1 on both terms. The header's Normal and CompactPerturbation are precisely the pointwise scalar equation and the quantified slab support hypothesis. This representation changes no original assumption or conclusion. In what follows all times under discussion lie strictly above zero.

2. Smooth calculus and mixed derivatives (B010, using B004, B005, B006).
Let w(x,t)=u(x,t)_k be one scalar coordinate, p=(x,t), T=(0,1) and X_j=(e_j,0). Scalar projection is a continuous linear map, so w is C∞ on U. The derivative of the affine time section r↦(x,r) is h↦(0,h); the derivative of y↦(y,t) is h↦(h,0). The chain rule therefore identifies V_k(p)=Dw(p)T and P_j,k(p)=Dw(p)X_j. These follow as HasDerivAt/HasFDerivAt statements first, followed by uniqueness of derivatives. Apply B006 on U, then evaluate at the fixed vector T or X_j, to see that these functions are again C∞ on U. Repeating B006 gives all the second derivatives and the regularity claimed here. These steps use only composition with continuous linear maps, the ordinary chain rule, and smoothness on an open domain.

For precision put H_p(v,w)=D(Dw)(p)(v)(w). Differentiating the fixed evaluations gives ∂_t P_j,k=H_p(T,X_j), ∂_j V_k=H_p(X_j,T), A_k=H_p(T,T) and S_j,k=H_p(X_j,X_j). B005, applied to the C² scalar w at p, says H_p(T,X_j)=H_p(X_j,T). Thus put W_j,k=∂_j V_k=∂_t P_j,k; this is an equality of actual derivatives of the functions already defined, not an additional PDE assumption. Each quantity and W_j is C∞ on U. Applying B004 to a scalar function multiplied by itself gives derivative 2f f'; differentiating finite coordinate sums and then the finite spatial sum yields
 d(x,t) := 2 dot(V(x,t),A(x,t)) + 2∑_j dot(P_j(x,t),W_j(x,t)),
 HasDerivAt (r↦e(x,r)) d(x,t) t.
Finite sums and products also show d is C∞ on U. This proves B010. The basic finite-sum, linear-map and chain-rule steps are ordinary internal calculus, with the whole pinned Mathlib available for their eventual Lean proofs; the prepared basis is not a restriction on theorem use.

3. Slab support and integrability (B011, using B001, B007, B010).
Fix any t₀>0. The original compactness hypothesis with s=t₀/2 and t=3t₀/2 is applicable since 0<t₀/2<3t₀/2. Choose its compact C and write J=[t₀/2,3t₀/2], I=(t₀/2,3t₀/2). A compact subset of the finite-dimensional real coordinate space is closed. Therefore O=Cᶜ×I is open. On O the original hypothesis says u=q. Around each point of O each scalar coordinate of u equals a constant on a neighborhood. B007 makes its Fréchet derivative zero. This equality holds throughout O, so the same locality argument applied again to that zero derivative makes the next derivatives zero. Inducting proves vanishing of all positive-order derivatives on O. Evaluating the spacetime derivatives in the directions in paragraph 2 gives V=A=P_j=S_j=W_j=0 there. In particular e and d vanish there.

For each r∈I, all of these quantities have continuous spatial sections by B010. Each displayed scalar section vanishes off C. Its ordinary support is therefore contained in C, and so is its closure because C is closed. Hence it has compact topological support. The same assertions hold for any finite sum or product of these sections, in particular V_k A_k, P_j,k W_j,k, V_k S_j,k, V_k P_j,k, W_j,k P_j,k, all their dot products and all finite sums used below. B001 makes every such scalar function integrable with respect to volume, and makes e(·,r) and d(·,r) integrable. This is also absolute integrability because these are real Bochner integrals. Taking r=t₀ and allowing arbitrary t₀>0 proves that the energy density is integrable at every requested time. Nothing about derivative vanishing at the time endpoints of J is asserted or needed.

4. Differentiation of the actual integral (B012, using B002, B008, B009, B010, B011).
Set η=t₀/4>0, K_t=[t₀−η,t₀+η] and s_t=(t₀−η,t₀+η). Direct inequalities from t₀>0 show K_t⊂I and s_t is a neighborhood of t₀. The product C×K_t is compact and lies in U. Continuity of d on this product and B008 give B₀ with |d(x,r)|≤B₀ for (x,r) in it. Put B=max(B₀,0) and b(x)=C.indicator(fun _↦B)(x). B009 makes b integrable. For x∈C and r∈s_t the compact bound gives |d(x,r)|≤b(x). For x∉C the left side is zero by paragraph 3 and the right side is zero. Thus the bound holds for every x and r∈s_t, in particular for ae x. This argument also handles C=∅ without choosing a maximum point.

Apply B002 with F(r,x)=e(x,r), F'(r,x)=d(x,r), basepoint t₀, neighborhood s_t, bound b. Here are all its hypotheses: s_t∈𝓝 t₀ as above; for all r∈s_t the spatial section e(·,r) is continuous and therefore ae strongly measurable, giving the required eventual measurability; e(·,t₀) is integrable by paragraph 3; d(·,t₀) is continuous and therefore ae strongly measurable; the derivative bound holds everywhere by the preceding cases; b is integrable by B009; and the pointwise HasDerivAt assertions for every r∈s_t follow from paragraph 2 because r>0. B002 concludes
 HasDerivAt E (∫ x, d(x,t₀)) t₀.
This proves differentiability of the original finite integral, rather than merely writing a formal derivative of an integral. The compact bound is local in t₀ and C, as allowed by the original hypotheses; it is not a new uniform bound on u over the whole half-space.

5. Tangency and the normality cancellation (B013, using B004, B010).
For fixed x, the unit constraint says ∑_k u_k(x,r)²=1 for every r>0. It therefore agrees locally with the constant 1 around every t>0. By B004 and the first derivative statements of paragraph 2, the derivative of this sum is 2∑_k u_k(x,t)V_k(x,t). Uniqueness of the derivative of a constant gives 2 dot(u,V)=0, hence dot(u,V)=0. Commutativity of real multiplication gives dot(V,u)=0. At just this (x,t), take a witness a from the original normality assumption A−L=a u. Finite-sum distributivity gives
 dot(V,A−L)=dot(V,a u)=a dot(V,u)=0.
No function selecting all witnesses is needed. In particular there is no continuity assumption on a and no differentiation of a. The supplied proof's optional explicit formula for a and its twice-differentiated constraint are unnecessary and are removed from the active proof.

6. Spatial integration by parts (B014, using B003, B010, B011).
Fix t₀>0, j∈Fin n and k∈Fin m. On the entire spatial coordinate space define f(x)=V_k(x,t₀) and g(x)=P_j,k(x,t₀), and take v=e_j. B010 makes f and g smooth, hence differentiable everywhere and in particular on the respective topological supports required by B003. Their directional derivatives are Df(x)e_j=W_j,k(x,t₀) and Dg(x)e_j=S_j,k(x,t₀). Each of (Df e_j)g, f(Dg e_j), and fg is continuous with compact support and integrable by paragraph 3. Thus every hypothesis of B003 is satisfied, giving
 ∫ x, V_k S_j,k = −∫ x, W_j,k P_j,k.
Sum over the finitely many k. The individual summands are integrable, so linearity commutes the sum and integral. Commuting real products inside the right integrand and changing the sign gives
 ∫ x, dot(P_j,W_j) = −∫ x, dot(V,S_j).
This is exactly the integration-by-parts identity used in the supplied proof, obtained directly from native whole-space integration by parts. No box-boundary or unproved multidimensional divergence theorem is introduced.

7. Assembly and normalization (B015, using B011–B014).
At the arbitrary t₀>0, paragraph 4 gives the derivative ∫ d. All of the following integral algebra has the integrability hypotheses from paragraph 3: finite sums, dot-product expansions, products, real scalar multiples and differences. Substitute the definition of d, then paragraph 6 for every j:
 ∫ d = 2∫ dot(V,A) + 2∑_j∫ dot(P_j,W_j)
      = 2∫ dot(V,A) − 2∑_j∫ dot(V,S_j)
      = 2∫ dot(V,A−∑_j S_j)
      = 2∫ dot(V,A−L) = 0.
The last equality is pointwise paragraph 5 followed by the integral of zero. Rewriting the derivative statement of paragraph 4 now gives HasDerivAt E 0 t₀. This includes differentiability and E'(t₀)=0. Paragraph 3 separately gives integrability at t₀. Since t₀>0 was arbitrary, all three requested conclusions hold at every positive time, with exactly coefficient 1 on |u_t|² and on each spatial derivative square. This establishes the full selected target; the usual constancy formulation of conservation is also a consequence of the zero derivative on the interval (0,∞). No assertion at time zero or altered PDE is used.

Dependency replacement record: the supplied difference-quotient/DCT calculation is replaced by native B002 plus the explicit B012 hypothesis verification; its compact bounding and integrability inputs are B001, B008, B009 and B011. The supplied box FTC/Fubini integration-by-parts argument is replaced by B003 with the explicit scalar applications in B014. Smooth differentiation and commuting mixed derivatives are resolved by B004–B006 and the concrete B010 construction. Local support reasoning is B007 followed by B011. Tangency and the PDE cancellation are proved internally in B013 and B015. Every category 3 item has a concrete derivation here from category 1 items through earlier category 3 items. There are no category 2 or 4 claims, no imported textbook assumptions, and no outstanding compatibility adapter. The Lean checks of category 1 declarations are compilation and trust checks; they are not mathematical approval of this natural-language proof or target correspondence.
header:
import Mathlib
open scoped Topology ContDiff
open MeasureTheory Filter
namespace WaveMapEnergy
abbrev Space (n : ℕ) := Fin n → ℝ
abbrev Value (m : ℕ) := Fin m → ℝ
def dot {m : ℕ} (v w : Value m) : ℝ := ∑ k, v k * w k
def normSq {m : ℕ} (v : Value m) : ℝ := dot v v
noncomputable def velocity {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => deriv (fun r => u (x, r) k) t
noncomputable def acceleration {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => deriv (fun r => velocity u x r k) t
noncomputable def spatial {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => fderiv ℝ (fun y => u (y, t) k) x (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def spatialSecond {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => fderiv ℝ (fun y => spatial u j y t k) x (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def laplacian {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m := ∑ j, spatialSecond u j x t
noncomputable def density {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  normSq (velocity u x t) + ∑ j, normSq (spatial u j x t)
noncomputable def energy {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x, density u x t
def Smooth {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ u {p | 0 < p.2}
def UnitValued {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  ∀ x t, 0 < t → normSq (u (x, t)) = 1
def Normal {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  ∀ x t, 0 < t → ∃ a : ℝ, acceleration u x t - laplacian u x t = a • u (x, t)
def CompactPerturbation {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) (q : Value m) : Prop :=
  ∀ s t : ℝ, 0 < s → s < t → ∃ C : Set (Space n), IsCompact C ∧
    ∀ x r, x ∉ C → r ∈ Set.Icc s t → u (x, r) = q
end WaveMapEnergy

replacements.original_dependency: Product rule for the unit constraint and the energy density
replacements.explanation: Use the native scalar product rule, finite coordinate sums and local equality to 1; the pointwise scalar witness is never differentiated.

replacements.original_dependency: Equality of mixed space and time derivatives and smoothness of derived fields
replacements.explanation: Express all derivatives through spacetime Fréchet derivatives and fixed affine injections; use C² symmetry on the open half-space.

replacements.original_dependency: Common compact support of derivatives, compact boundedness and integrability
replacements.explanation: Obtain local constancy on the open complement of the original slab compact set, then derivative vanishing, compact spatial supports, integrability and the compact indicator bound.

replacements.original_dependency: Differentiation under the integral by mean value theorem and dominated convergence
replacements.explanation: Apply the native dominated derivative theorem; B012 checks every assumption using the original locally uniform slab support.

replacements.original_dependency: Spatial integration by parts through box FTC and Fubini
replacements.explanation: Apply native scalar directional whole-space integration by parts to each target coordinate, with all integrability and differentiability premises proved from the original H.
The formula is unnecessary. Tangency plus pointwise normality gives exactly the cancellation needed, preserving the weaker assumption that only a scalar witness exists at each point.

replacements.original_dependency: Final finite-sum integral algebra and cancellation
replacements.explanation: All terms are integrable; substitute integration by parts into the actual energy derivative and use dot(V,A−L)=0 pointwise.

B003.statement: For every n, differentiable scalar functions f,g on ℝⁿ and direction v, if (Df·v)g, f(Dg·v), and fg are Lebesgue integrable, then ∫ f(Dg·v) = -∫ (Df·v)g. It suffices that f is differentiable at every point of tsupport g and g at every point of tsupport f.

B010.statement: For all n,m≥1 and u : Space n×ℝ → Value m with Smooth u, let V=velocity u, A=acceleration u, P_j=spatial u j, S_j=spatialSecond u j, and W_j(x,t)_k=fderiv ℝ (y↦velocity u y t k) x (Pi.single j 1). All these maps are C∞ on t>0. For each k,j,x and t>0, HasDerivAt (r↦u(x,r)_k) V(x,t)_k t, HasDerivAt (r↦V(x,r)_k) A(x,t)_k t and HasDerivAt (r↦P_j(x,r)_k) W_j(x,t)_k t hold. The spatial Fréchet derivatives of u_k and P_j,k in direction e_j equal P_j,k and S_j,k by definition. Writing d(x,t)=2 dot(V,A)+2∑_j dot(P_j,W_j), HasDerivAt (r↦density u x r) d(x,t) t holds, and d is C∞ on t>0. The header's coordinate representation, normSq, Laplacian and volume agree with the original Euclidean target and Lebesgue measure; no extension across t=0 is required to be smooth.

origin.reference: Proof paragraphs 1–2: coordinate representation and spacetime differentiation

B010.justification: Apply open-set smooth derivative closure to scalar coordinate projections, restrict derivatives along affine time/spatial injections, evaluate continuous linear maps at fixed directions, and use second-derivative symmetry for the two mixed directions. Product-rule differentiation and finite sums give d. Full derivation is in the proof.

B011.statement: For all n,m≥1, u,q with Smooth u and CompactPerturbation u q, every t₀>0 admits a compact C and J=[t₀/2,3t₀/2] such that u=q on Cᶜ×J. On Cᶜ×int J all positive-order derivatives of u vanish. For every r∈int J, all scalar components of V,A,P_j,S_j,W_j, density e, d from B010, and the products V_k A_k, P_j,k W_j,k, V_k S_j,k, V_k P_j,k and W_j,k P_j,k are continuous spatial functions with compact support in C and are Lebesgue integrable. In particular density u (·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

origin.reference: Proof paragraph 3: support locality and integrability

B011.justification: At a point outside the closed compact C and at an interior time, an open product neighborhood has u=q. Locality makes first derivatives zero throughout that open set, and iteration gives all positive derivatives zero. A continuous section vanishing outside closed compact C has topological support contained in C; apply B001.

B012.statement: For all n,m≥1, u,q with Smooth u and CompactPerturbation u q, and every t₀>0, HasDerivAt (energy u) (∫ x, d(x,t₀)) t₀, where d is the explicit density derivative in B010. Thus the actual finite Lebesgue energy integral is differentiable on (0,∞).

origin.reference: Proof paragraph 4: uniform compact bound and differentiation under the integral

B012.justification: Use the C from B011, η=t₀/4 and compact C×[t₀-η,t₀+η]. B008 bounds |d| there; max(B,0)1_C is an integrable bound by B009 and d=0 off C. All measurability, integrability and pointwise derivative assumptions of B002 are checked in the proof.

B013.statement: For all n,m≥1 and Smooth, UnitValued u, dot(u(x,t),velocity u x t)=0 for all x and t>0. If also Normal u, then dot(velocity u x t, acceleration u x t-laplacian u x t)=0 for every such point. The pointwise normality witnesses a are neither differentiated nor assumed continuous.

origin.reference: Proof paragraph 5: differentiated constraint and pointwise normality

B013.justification: The derivative of ∑_k u_k²=1 is 2∑_k u_k V_k=0 by B004 and B010, giving tangency by real arithmetic. Select only the scalar a at the current point and substitute A-L=a u into its dot product with V.

B014.statement:
For all n,m≥1, Smooth u and CompactPerturbation u q, each t₀>0 and j∈Fin n satisfy
∫ x, dot(spatial u j x t₀, W_j(x,t₀)) = -∫ x, dot(velocity u x t₀, spatialSecond u j x t₀),
where W_j is defined in B010. All integrands and the auxiliary products required for integration by parts are Lebesgue integrable.

origin.reference: Proof paragraph 6: componentwise spatial integration by parts

B014.justification: For each target coordinate k apply B003 with f=V_k(·,t₀), g=P_j,k(·,t₀), direction e_j. All three integrability assumptions come from B011 and differentiability from B010. Sum the resulting identities over k and commute products.

B015.statement: For every n,m∈ℕ with n≥1,m≥1, every u : Space n×ℝ → Value m and q : Value m satisfying normSq q=1, Smooth u, UnitValued u, Normal u and CompactPerturbation u q, and every t>0, density u (·,t) is Lebesgue integrable and HasDerivAt (energy u) 0 t. In particular energy u is differentiable at every positive time and deriv (energy u) t=0. Through the representation in B010 this is exactly the full selected target with e=|u_t|²+∑_j|∂_j u|² and E=∫ e, without any assertion at zero.

origin.reference: Proof paragraph 7: finite integral algebra and cancellation

B015.justification: Insert B014 into the integral expression in B012. The derivative integral becomes 2∫ dot(V,A-∑_j S_j), whose integrand is zero pointwise by B013. B011 supplies every integrability hypothesis for distributing all finite sums, scalar factors and differences.
